Prepare a negotiation from your life or work: the other side's position and interest, your interests, your walk-away point, your best alternative, what you can trade, and the order.
exercicios.frase: walk-away point
exercicios.resposta: I'm renewing my rent. The landlord's position is a twenty percent increase; his interest is a reliable tenant. My walk-away point is ten percent. My best alternative is a smaller flat nearby. I can trade a two-year contract, and I'll keep paying in advance in reserve.

exercicios.enunciado: Is it a good idea to tell the other side your walk-away point? Why, or why not?
exercicios.frase: because
exercicios.resposta: Usually not, because they'll offer exactly that and no more. But sometimes, near the end, saying "below this, we walk away" honestly can unblock an impasse.

exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita, devagar e com a voz baixa.
Think of a negotiation that got stuck. Describe the impasse and one pressure tactic, and say what you would say to unblock it, with at least four expressions from this lesson.
exercicios.frase: step back
exercicios.resposta: When I bought my car, we were going round in circles on price. Then the seller said another buyer was coming at five. I'd say: "I understand, but I can't agree to that under pressure. Let's take a step back. What would it take for you to move?"

exercicios.enunciado: Are pressure tactics ever acceptable in a negotiation? Where is the line?
exercicios.frase: line
exercicios.resposta: A real deadline is fair; a false one isn't. I'd draw the line at lying: inventing another buyer or a board meeting that doesn't exist. That damages trust for the next deal.

Sum up an agreement you know or imagine (a rent, a job offer, a purchase) in four or five precise points, each with its condition, and end with a confirmation question.
exercicios.frase: understanding
exercicios.resposta: Just to confirm: the salary is three hundred thousand kwanzas a month, with effect from February. The company pays my English course, on condition that I stay two years. In the event of a transfer, housing is paid for six months. Is that your understanding too?

exercicios.enunciado: Is it better to agree on a short summary and trust each other, or to write everything down in detail? Why?
exercicios.frase: because
exercicios.resposta: Write it down, because memory changes and people leave. A clear summary protects the relationship: nobody has to argue later about what was said.

Negotiate something small with a friend (a shared lunch, a gift, a trip, a flat) using at least five C1 structures naturally: a cleft, a hedge, an inversion, a participle clause, ellipsis, fronting, a marker, a summary.
exercicios.frase: What I
exercicios.resposta: What I'd suggest is splitting the trip by days. It would appear you're staying four days and I'm staying six. Having looked at the prices, that's fairer. Mind you, you'll drive: never have I seen anyone park like you! So, just to confirm: hotel by days, car half each.

exercicios.enunciado: Which C1 structure do you find most useful in real life? Why?
exercicios.frase: because
exercicios.resposta: Cleft sentences, because they put the important idea where people notice it: "What we need is…". I use them in meetings every week now.

Describe a deal you know with at least six words from this lesson: the sticking point, a deal-breaker, the sweetener, who had leverage, how they met halfway, and when it became a done deal.
exercicios.frase: sticking point
exercicios.resposta: When my uncle sold his shop, the main sticking point was the stock. For him, including it all was a deal-breaker. The buyer had leverage, but they met halfway: half the stock. The sweetener was a month of training. By Friday, it was a done deal.

exercicios.enunciado: Who usually has more leverage in a negotiation, the buyer or the seller? Why?
exercicios.frase: leverage
exercicios.resposta: Whoever has the better alternative has more leverage. If there are many sellers, the buyer has it; if the product is rare, the seller has it.

licoes.objectivo: Seguir uma negociação com intérprete e perceber onde quase falhou.

exercicios.frase: I'm the narrator. A logistics company wants to rent two warehouses at a port for ten years.
exercicios.enunciado: How long does the company want to rent the warehouses?

exercicios.frase: I'm Karen Visser. We're ready to sign for ten years, provided that we can bring in our own forklift drivers for the first year.
exercicios.enunciado: What does Ms Visser want for the first year?

opcoes.texto: to bring in her own forklift drivers

exercicios.frase: This is Benvinda, the interpreter. Mr Macamo says: our pretensions are simple, local workers from day one.
exercicios.enunciado: Which word caused the problem?

exercicios.frase: I'm Karen Visser. Our concern is safety: our machines are new, and an accident in the first month would be a disaster.
exercicios.enunciado: What is Ms Visser's real concern?

exercicios.frase: I'm Jaime Cossa. Suppose your drivers train ours for the first three months, side by side?
exercicios.enunciado: What does Mr Cossa propose?

opcoes.texto: that her drivers train local drivers for three months

exercicios.frase: This is Karen Visser. Local drivers trained by ours for three months, then local drivers only, subject to our safety test.
exercicios.enunciado: What happens after three months?

opcoes.texto: local drivers only, if they pass the safety test

exercicios.enunciado: Who saved the deal?

opcoes.texto: Mr Cossa, who spoke both languages, and the interpreter, who admitted her mistake

exercicios.enunciado: "Something got lost in translation." This means…

opcoes.texto: The meaning changed when it was translated.

exercicios.frase: I think something got lost in translation.
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita em voz alta.

exercicios.frase: Then we're not so far apart.
exercicios.enunciado: Ouça e repita em voz alta.
You are the negotiation instructor. Explain what went wrong, who saved the deal and how, and give one piece of advice for negotiating across two languages.
exercicios.frase: lost in translation
exercicios.resposta: The interpreter translated "pretensões" as "pretensions", which means vanity, and Ms Visser felt insulted. Mr Cossa said something got lost in translation. They went back to interests: jobs and safety. My advice: ask before you react.

exercicios.enunciado: Should important negotiations use a professional interpreter, or is it better if one person speaks both languages? Why?
exercicios.frase: interpreter
exercicios.resposta: Both, ideally. A professional interpreter is neutral, but someone who knows both cultures notices when a word sounds wrong. In this case, that person saved the deal.

Close a negotiation with two other parties: open with the common interests, unblock one impasse, refuse one last-minute demand with an alternative, and sum up the deal in four precise points, ending with a confirmation question.
exercicios.frase: everyone's understanding
exercicios.resposta: We all want a clean, affordable market. Let's take a step back: the council pays the roof, the sellers pay the cleaning. Free parking every day is a deal-breaker; Sundays we can do. So: rent from January, roof, cleaning, Sunday parking. Is that everyone's understanding?

exercicios.enunciado: Tell the others, in English, what this partner said: "Quero ser claro: a nossa associação não aceita aumentos de renda este ano. Se o mercado ficar mais limpo e seguro, podemos falar de um aumento no próximo ano, mas só depois de uma reunião com todos os vendedores."
exercicios.frase: wants to be clear
exercicios.resposta: He wants to be clear: their association won't accept any rent increase this year. If the market becomes cleaner and safer, they could talk about an increase next year, but only after a meeting with all the sellers.

exercicios.enunciado: Describe the most difficult negotiation you have had or seen. What were the interests behind the positions?
exercicios.frase: interest
exercicios.resposta: My hardest negotiation was with my brother about our parents' house. His position was to sell; mine was to keep it. His interest was money for his children's studies; mine was a place for the family. We found a deal: rent it out.

exercicios.enunciado: Looking back at the whole course, what has changed most in the way you speak English?
exercicios.frase: changed
exercicios.resposta: What has changed most is my confidence. At the start, I translated every sentence from Portuguese. Now I choose how to say things: formally, diplomatically, or with friends, more relaxed.
